problems.title: Area between two graphs

publicContent.stem: Compute the area between the graphs of $y=x^2$ and $y=-2x+3$. Show all your work.

grading.analysis: The intersection points satisfy $x^2=-2x+3$, so $x^2+2x-3=0$ and $(x+3)(x-1)=0$. Thus the curves intersect at $x=-3$ and $x=1$. On this interval, the line is above the parabola because at $x=0$, $-2(0)+3=3>0=x^2$. Therefore the area is $\int_{-3}^{1}((-2x+3)-x^2)\,dx=\left[-\frac{x^3}{3}-x^2+3x\right]_{-3}^{1}=\frac{32}{3}$.

problems.title: Indefinite integral with powers of x

publicContent.stem: Evaluate the following integral. Show all your work. $\int \frac{x^2+1+x^{-2}}{x}\,dx$

grading.analysis: Rewrite the integrand as $\frac{x^2+1+x^{-2}}{x}=x+x^{-1}+x^{-3}$. Integrating term by term gives $\frac{x^2}{2}+\ln\lvert x\rvert-\frac{1}{2}x^{-2}+C$, equivalently $\frac{x^2}{2}+\ln\lvert x\rvert-\frac{1}{2x^2}+C$.

problems.title: Partial-fraction integral

publicContent.stem: Evaluate the following integral. Show all your work. $\int \frac{1}{x^3-x}\,dx$

grading.analysis: Factor the denominator: $x^3-x=x(x-1)(x+1)$. Use the decomposition $\frac{1}{x(x-1)(x+1)}=-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{2(x-1)}+\frac{1}{2(x+1)}$. Integrating gives $-\ln\lvert x\rvert+\frac{1}{2}\ln\lvert x-1\rvert+\frac{1}{2}\ln\lvert x+1\rvert+C$.

problems.title: Definite trigonometric integral

publicContent.stem: Evaluate the following integral. Show all your work. $\int_{0}^{\pi/4}x\sin 2x\,dx$

grading.analysis: Use integration by parts with $u=x$ and $dv=\sin 2x\,dx$, so $du=dx$ and $v=-\frac{1}{2}\cos 2x$. Thus $\int x\sin 2x\,dx=-\frac{x}{2}\cos 2x+\frac{1}{4}\sin 2x$. Evaluating from $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{4}$ gives $\left[-\frac{x}{2}\cos 2x+\frac{1}{4}\sin 2x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}=\frac{1}{4}$.

problems.title: Definite integral involving a square root

publicContent.stem: Evaluate the following integral. Show all your work. $\int_{1}^{9}\frac{dx}{x+\sqrt{x}}$

grading.analysis: Let $t=\sqrt{x}$, so $x=t^2$ and $dx=2t\,dt$. The denominator becomes $t^2+t=t(t+1)$, so the integrand becomes $\frac{2t}{t(t+1)}\,dt=\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt$. The bounds change from $x=1,9$ to $t=1,3$. Therefore the integral is $\int_{1}^{3}\frac{2}{t+1}\,dt=2\ln(t+1)\big\vert_{1}^{3}=2\ln 2$.

problems.title: Calculation of Calculus

publicContent.stem: Find $F'(x)$ for $x>0$ if $F(x)=\int_{0}^{x^2}\sqrt{t}\sin\sqrt{t}\,dt.$ Show all your work.

grading.analysis: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule, $F'(x)=\sqrt{x^2}\sin\sqrt{x^2}\cdot 2x$. Since $x>0$, $\sqrt{x^2}=x$. Hence $F'(x)=2x^2\sin x$.

publicContent.stem: Determine $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(i/n)^2}}.$ Show all of your work.

grading.analysis:
The sum has the form $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(i/n)\,\Delta x$ with $\Delta x=1/n$ and $f(x)=1/\sqrt{1+x^2}$.
The sample points $i/n$ run from $1/n$ to $1$, so the limit is the right-endpoint Riemann sum for $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\,dx$.
An antiderivative is $\operatorname{arsinh}(x)=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)$.
Evaluating gives $\operatorname{arsinh}(1)-\operatorname{arsinh}(0)=\ln(1+\sqrt{2})$.

problems.title: Definite integral of secant and tangent

publicContent.stem: Evaluate $\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\sec^2 x\tan x\,dx.$ Show all of your work.

grading.analysis:
Use the substitution $u=\tan x$, so $du=\sec^2 x\,dx$.
The integral becomes $\int_{\tan(\pi/4)}^{\tan(\pi/3)}u\,du=\frac{1}{2}u^2\big|_1^{\sqrt{3}}$.
Therefore the value is $\frac{1}{2}(3-1)=1$.

problems.title: Volume of a rotated circular region

publicContent.stem: Find the volume of the solid that results when the region inside the curve $(x-2)^2+y^2=1$ is rotated about the $y$ -axis. Show all of your work.

grading.analysis:
The curve encloses a disk of radius $1$ centered at $(2,0)$.
When this disk is revolved about the $y$ -axis, its centroid travels a distance $2\pi(2)=4\pi$.
The area of the generating region is $\pi(1)^2=\pi$.
By Pappus's centroid theorem, the volume is $(4\pi)(\pi)=4\pi^2$ cubic units.
Equivalently, using cylindrical shells, $V=\int_1^3 2\pi x\sqrt{1-(x-2)^2}\,dx=4\pi^2$.

publicContent.stem: Suppose $f(x)$ is a function satisfying $\lvert f''(x)\rvert\le 2\quad\text{for }0\le x\le 3.$ How large should $n$ be in order that the midpoint rule applied to $\int_0^3 f(x)\,dx$ be accurate to within $10^{-2}$? Show all of your work.

grading.analysis:
For the midpoint rule, if $\lvert f''(x)\rvert\le K$ on $[a,b]$, the error satisfies $\lvert E_M\rvert\le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}$.
Here $K=2$, $a=0$, and $b=3$, so $\lvert E_M\rvert\le \frac{2(3)^3}{24n^2}=\frac{9}{4n^2}$.
Require $\frac{9}{4n^2}\le 10^{-2}$. Multiplying by $n^2$ and solving gives $n^2\ge 225$, hence $n\ge 15$.
Since $n$ must be a positive integer, the smallest sufficient value is $n=15$.

sourceAnchors.textQuote: (a) Give a careful definition of the definite integral ∫ from a to b f(x) dx.

publicContent.explanation: Partition the interval $[a,b]$ by $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$. Choose a sample point $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ in each subinterval and define the mesh by $\lVert P\rVert=\max_i(x_i-x_{i-1})$. Form the tagged Riemann sum $S(f,P,\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^n f(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})$. The definite integral exists and equals $I$ when all tagged Riemann sums approach the same number $I$ as the mesh tends to zero; equivalently, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $\lVert P\rVert<\delta$ implies $\lvert S(f,P,\xi)-I\rvert<\varepsilon$ for every choice of tags.
publicContent.stem: Give a careful definition of the definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$ Include the partition, sample points, Riemann sum, and limiting condition. Show all of your work.

grading.referenceProof:
Let $P$ be a partition of $[a,b]$ of the form $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$. Choose a tag or sample point $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$ for each subinterval, and define the mesh of the partition by

$\lVert P\rVert=\max_{1\le i\le n}(x_i-x_{i-1}).$

The corresponding tagged Riemann sum is $S(f;P,\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(\xi_i)(x_i-x_{i-1}).$ A function $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ if there exists a real number $I$ such that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a $\delta>0$ with the property that for every partition $P$ and every choice of tags $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$, if $\lVert P\rVert<\delta$, then

$\left|S(f;P,\xi)-I\right|<\varepsilon.$

The definite integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$ is defined to be this common limit:

$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=I=\lim_{\lVert P\rVert\to0}S(f;P,\xi),$

where the limit is required to be the same for every choice of sample points.

rubricCriteria.description: Defines a partition $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_n=b$ and sample points $\xi_i\in[x_{i-1},x_i]$.

States that the integral is the common limit as the mesh tends to zero.
Gives a correct quantified $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limiting condition and identifies the limit as $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.

publicContent.explanation: Use the standard two-part Fundamental Theorem of Calculus under the hypothesis that $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. Part I: Define $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$. For $h\ne0$, $\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt$. By continuity of $f$ at $x$, the average value of $f$ over the interval between $x$ and $x+h$ approaches $f(x)$ as $h\to0$. Hence $F'(x)=f(x)$. Part II: Let $G$ be any antiderivative of $f$, so $G'=f$. Since Part I gives $F'=f$, the function $H=G-F$ satisfies $H'=0$, hence is constant. Therefore $G(b)-G(a)=F(b)-F(a)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
publicContent.stem: State and prove the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Include the hypotheses, the theorem statement, and a complete proof.

grading.referenceProof:
Assume that $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a,b]$.

Part I: Define $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ by $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt.$ Then $F$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $F'(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in(a,b)$. Indeed, for $h$ such that $x+h\in[a,b]$ and $h\ne0$,

$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt.$

Subtracting $f(x)$ gives

$\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}-f(x)=\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h}(f(t)-f(x))\,dt.$

Because $f$ is continuous at $x$, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|t-x|<\delta$. If $|h|<\delta$, the absolute value of the last average is at most $\varepsilon$. Therefore the difference quotient tends to $f(x)$ as $h\to0$, so $F'(x)=f(x)$.

Part II: If $G$ is any antiderivative of $f$ on $[a,b]$, then $G'(x)=f(x)$. From Part I, $F'(x)=f(x)$, so the function $H=G-F$ satisfies $H'(x)=G'(x)-F'(x)=0$ on $(a,b)$. By the mean value theorem, $H$ is constant on $[a,b]$. Hence $G(b)-F(b)=G(a)-F(a)$, which implies $G(b)-G(a)=F(b)-F(a)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$ Thus, under the stated continuity hypothesis, $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt=f(x)$ and, for every antiderivative $G$ of $f$, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=G(b)-G(a)$.

rubricCriteria.description: States appropriate continuity and differentiability hypotheses and states both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Proves Part I by forming the difference quotient for $F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ and showing it tends to $f(x)$.
Proves Part II by comparing an antiderivative $G$ with $F$ and showing that $G-F$ is constant.
Correctly concludes $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=G(b)-G(a)$ and presents a logically complete argument.
